ol96b1-277864.summary: Auriol's question whether God is everywhere by essence, presence and power, the scholastic commentary on Lombard's distinction 37. Opening arguments deny omnipresence: being-in is not reciprocal and all things are in God; God is above all and 'nowhere'; he abstracts from place as from time (Anselm, Augustine, Damascene); 'where' is not a divine category; even unity and the now abstract from place; new presence would change God; and he is only an extrinsic cause. Patristic authorities (Gregory, Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose) and Scripture affirm it. Article 1 asks what omnipresence formally is and rejects Thomas (presence as operation), Scotus (a real relation of presence distinct from operation, with action at a distance possible), Richard of Middleton (infinite spiritual magnitude), Durand (an order of coexistence), and the simultaneity view. Auriol's thesis is that God is everywhere by complete non-distance (indistantia), a negative condition without nearness, contact or within-ness, determined by operation, which requires its power to be non-distant; so only God, acting everywhere, is everywhere. Article 2 asks whether this is demonstrable. Operation does not prove positive presence, since the heavens are moved by an abstract power, but it does prove non-distance, since no power acts at a distance; bodily action diffuses through the medium, and substantial forms are educed through alteration. Scotus's counterexamples (the sun) are answered, and given the faith-held premise of universal conservation, omnipresence follows demonstratively on supposition, on the model of Aristotle's first mover. Article 3 makes essence, presence and power substrate, formal character and determinant of one mode; explains immensity (deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place), illapsus and containment (all things are in God because of their dependence); and reduces presence by grace to the same mode singularized by grace's intense operation, with Christ's presence grounded in the hypostatic union. The replies apply the theory of non-distance throughout.
claims: God is everywhere by complete non-distance (indistantia), not by any positive relation of presence, simultaneity, order or magnitude.
Omnipresence is not formally operation, though operation determines non-distance.
No power acts immediately at a distance; operation proves the non-distance of its power.
Given universal conservation (held by faith), omnipresence is demonstrable on supposition.
Essence, presence and power are substrate, formal character and determinant of one mode.
Immensity is deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place.
Presence by grace is the same mode singularized by grace's operation; presence in Christ follows from the hypostatic union.
God's becoming present to new creatures involves no change in him.

ol96b1-277864-d1e107.summary: Title of the question: whether God is everywhere by essence, presence and power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e114.summary: Ties the question to Lombard's treatment of how God is in things and opens the arguments that he is not everywhere. First: modes of being-in are not reciprocal (if wine is in the jar, the jar is not in the wine, Physics IV), and all things are in God ('in him we live, move and are', Acts 17; Bede: wherever an angel moves it is within God). So God cannot conversely be in all things.
claims: (Argument) Being-in is not reciprocal, and all things are in God.

ol96b1-277864-d1e146.summary: Argues that opposites cannot belong to the same thing, and God is outside and above all (Psalm 112; 'God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere', Book of the 24 Philosophers). God's circumference is God, so God is nowhere and not everywhere.
claims: (Argument) God is beyond all things and so nowhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e168.summary: Argues that God abstracts from place as from time, and he is above time, not in it (Liber de causis), so he is above place, not in it.
claims: (Argument) God is above place as he is above time.

ol96b1-277864-d1e179.summary: Argues from Anselm: it would be more fitting to say God is with place or time than in them, and he is properly in no place or time, which would be false if he were everywhere.
claims: (Argument) God is properly in no place (Anselm).

ol96b1-277864-d1e195.summary: Argues that what is not somewhere is not everywhere, and Augustine (83 Questions) says God is not somewhere; rather all things are in him, and he is neither a place nor in a place.
claims: (Argument) God is not somewhere, so not everywhere (Augustine).

ol96b1-277864-d1e208.summary: Argues that only substance and relation among the categories apply to God (Boethius, De Trinitate), but 'being everywhere' belongs to the category 'where', answering 'where?' with 'here', 'there' or 'everywhere'.
claims: (Argument) Only substance and relation are predicated of God.

ol96b1-277864-d1e230.summary: Argues that God is more abstract than any creature, and some creatures abstract wholly from place (unity lacks position, Posterior Analytics I; the 'now' is not beyond or this side of the sea). So God is not in place or everywhere.
claims: (Argument) Even some creatures, like unity and the now, abstract from place.

ol96b1-277864-d1e251.summary: Argues that nothing implying change can be posited in God (no change per se or per accidens in the first mover, Metaphysics XII, Physics VIII). If God were everywhere, when a stone is created he would begin to be in it, passing from contradictory to contradictory, which requires change in what passes.
claims: (Argument) Beginning to be in new things would change God.

ol96b1-277864-d1e280.summary: Argues that God is an extrinsic cause of things (efficient and final, not matter or form) and is in things only as their cause, so he is not properly in them.
claims: (Argument) God is only an extrinsic cause and so not properly in things.

ol96b1-277864-d1e298.summary: Argues from John Damascene: God, being immaterial, is not in place; he is his own place and, being above all, contains all. This would be false if God were somewhere or everywhere.
claims: (Argument) God is his own place (Damascene).

ol96b1-277864-d1e311.summary: Rubric for the arguments that God is everywhere by essence, presence and power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e318.summary: Argues from authority that God is everywhere: Gregory (on the Song of Songs), that God is in all things by presence, power and substance and in the saints by grace; Augustine (De praesentia Dei), that God, incorporeal, is wholly present to all and to each; Hilary, that God of immense power is nowhere absent. These require presence by essence, not only power.
claims: (Argument) The Fathers teach that God is present to all things by essence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e349.summary: Argues that whatever suffices to prove something is God belongs truly to God, and Ambrose proves the Holy Spirit is not a creature because he is everywhere.
claims: (Argument) Being everywhere is proper to God (Ambrose).

ol96b1-277864-d1e366.summary: Argues that whatever signifies perfection and infinity belongs to God, and immensity, by which God is in all things, does ('I fill heaven and earth', Jeremiah 23; 'reaches from end to end mightily', Wisdom 8).
claims: (Argument) Immensity is a perfection to be attributed to God.

ol96b1-277864-d1e384.summary: Rubric marking the response to the question.

ol96b1-277864-d1e395.summary: Introduces the order of the response.

ol96b1-277864-d1e402.summary: First step: what 'God is everywhere' formally means.

ol96b1-277864-d1e409.summary: Second step: whether God's being everywhere can be demonstrated from the operation by which he conserves and sustains creatures.

ol96b1-277864-d1e418.summary: Third step: the distinction of the commonly assigned modes of being: by essence, power, presence and grace.

ol96b1-277864-Dd1e428.summary: Asks what 'God is everywhere' formally means. Opinions: Thomas (being everywhere just is operating everywhere, since agent and patient are together and being is God's intimate proper effect); Scotus (operation does not prove presence, since more perfect agents act at a distance as the sun does; presence of essence is a real relation in creatures, distinct from and posterior to operation); Richard of Middleton (positive infinite spiritual magnitude); Durand (an order of real coexistence presupposed by operation); and others (God is in place only by presence, a real relation of simultaneity in creatures). Auriol's five propositions. God's presence is not a relation of simultaneity, since simultaneity needs a common foundation in time, place or position, which God lacks, presupposes position, and would give God an inside and outside. It is not a relation of order, causal or positional. It is not formally operation, which would make presence by essence the metaphorical presence of power, as a king in his realm, against Lombard, the question test and Augustine. It is not spiritual magnitude, whether extensive (quantity) or intensive (irrelevant to place). God is in things by retaining only the negative condition of the located toward place: complete non-distance, without nearness, contact or within-ness. This non-distance is determined by operation, which requires that its power not be distant, so only God, acting everywhere, is everywhere (Damascene, Aristotle, Averroes). Objections are answered: non-distance without nearness is possible, angels act only locally, and the saints' positive language reflects the difficulty of thinking beyond imagination.
claims: God's omnipresence is not simultaneity, order, operation, or spiritual magnitude.
God is everywhere by complete non-distance (indistantia) from all things, a negative condition.
Operation determines non-distance from its effects, so only God, operating everywhere, is everywhere.
The saints' language of positive presence accommodates the difficulty of abstract thought.

ol96b1-277864-d1e437.summary: Rubric naming Thomas Aquinas's opinion (ST I q. 8 a. 1 and 2).

ol96b1-277864-d1e442.summary: States Thomas's view: God is in things because his power actually reaches their innermost being, since agent and patient must be together (Physics VII). God, being subsistent being itself, has being as his proper effect, and being is most intimate in each thing, so God is most intimate to each, causing and conserving its being. A bodily agent, circumscribed by quantity, is with its effect only by contact and acts through intermediaries; a spiritual agent, abstract from quantity and place, cannot be separated by place from what it moves, so it is where the moved is (the soul in the body, the heaven's mover in its right side). So God, the most abstract agent, is in things by his operation, and being everywhere formally just is operating everywhere.
claims: (Reported) Agent and patient must be together.
(Reported) Being is God's proper effect and most intimate to things.
(Reported) A spiritual agent is wherever it acts.
(Reported) For God, being everywhere formally is operating everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e514.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio I d. 37 q. un.).

ol96b1-277864-d1e520.summary: States Scotus's objection: God's continual operation in creatures' innermost being does not prove he is in them, since the more perfect an agent, the more it can act at a distance from the form by which it acts. The sun produces substantial forms not through its ray but immediately by its form, the ray only altering; otherwise the effect would exceed its cause. God, the most perfect agent, can act on what is distant.
claims: (Reported) More perfect agents can act at greater distance.
(Reported) The sun induces substantial forms immediately by its form, not by its rays.

ol96b1-277864-d1e564.summary: Continues Scotus: the reply that the ray induces the form by the sun's power fails. Either that power is an accident in the ray, which cannot induce a nobler substantial form, or it is the sun's form itself, which then acts where it is not present.
claims: (Reported) Either an accident induces a nobler form, or the sun acts where it is not.

ol96b1-277864-d1e586.summary: Continues Scotus: whatever perfection belongs to the sun belongs a fortiori to God, and the sun acts where it is not, even through no medium: 'man and the sun generate man' even when the sun is in the other hemisphere, and metals form deep in the earth where neither rays nor reflected heat reach. So God can act where he is not.
claims: (Reported) The sun acts where neither it nor its rays are present.

ol96b1-277864-d1e617.summary: Continues Scotus: an omnipotent being causes by willing, and willing does not require being joined to what is willed, so what God wills can be produced without his essence being in it.
claims: (Reported) God causes by will, which needs no presence to its object.

ol96b1-277864-d1e633.summary: Continues Scotus: what is prior can be separated from what is posterior, and presence by operation and power is prior to presence of essence. God can act outside the world where his essence is not, and the creature must exist by nature before the essence is present to it, existing then only through divine action. So the essence need not be present because it acts intimately.
claims: (Reported) Presence by operation is prior to presence by essence and separable from it.

ol96b1-277864-d1e664.summary: Continues Scotus: what the philosophers denied should not be attributed to God on account of operation. They posited two movers for each orb, one in a determinate part (the east), the other, of infinite power and identical with God, in no place or position. So a mover need not be in what it moves.
claims: (Reported) The philosophers' supreme mover moves without being in a place.

ol96b1-277864-d1e689.summary: Continues Scotus: passage between contradictories requires change in something. God becomes present to a new creature not by change in himself but by the creature's production, so production is understood before presence of essence and is not its formal ground.
claims: (Reported) God's new presence results from the creature's production, which is prior.

ol96b1-277864-d1e713.summary: Continues Scotus: 'mover and moved are together' (Physics VII) concerns bodies in contact by active and passive qualities, without one being in the other by essence. The question here is presence by essence, so the text does not apply.
claims: (Reported) Physics VII's principle concerns contact of qualities, not presence of essence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e744.summary: Continues Scotus: a natural agent cannot act on a distant thing without first acting on the medium, for two possible reasons.

ol96b1-277864-d1e753.summary: First reason: the order of powers. The sun's substantial form cannot introduce substantial forms until its light alters by irradiation, though it does not act on the medium by the same action by which it generates minerals and plants at a distance, just as the will cannot act until the intellect has.
claims: (Reported) An order of powers can require prior action on the medium.

ol96b1-277864-d1e779.summary: Second reason: the imperfection of an active power that must proceed from imperfect to perfect, so it acts on the medium before the distant patient. Remove both (order and imperfection), as in God's omnipotence, and there is no reason a power cannot act where it is not present. So God can act where he is not.
claims: (Reported) Without order of powers and imperfection, an agent can act at a distance.
(Reported) Omnipotence lacks both constraints.

ol96b1-277864-d1e805.summary: Concludes Scotus's view: though God is everywhere and his action reaches everywhere, his action does not make him present everywhere by essence. He is everywhere by the presence of his essence to all things, which differs from operation and can be a real relation in the creature terminating at the divine essence.
claims: (Reported) God is everywhere by presence of essence, distinct from operation.
(Reported) This presence is a real relation in creatures terminating at God.

ol96b1-277864-d1e828.summary: Rubric naming Richard of Middleton's opinion (Sentences I d. 37 q. 3).

ol96b1-277864-d1e833.summary: States Richard's view: God is everywhere because of his positive spiritual immensity. There are four kinds of simplicity, listed next.
claims: (Reported) God is everywhere by positive spiritual immensity.

ol96b1-277864-d1e844.summary: First simplicity: negative of magnitude, as in a point, neither extended nor apt to be.

ol96b1-277864-d1e853.summary: Second simplicity: privative of magnitude, as in bodily substance separated from its dimensions by divine power, apt to be extended but not extended.

ol96b1-277864-d1e866.summary: Third simplicity: positive spiritual magnitude without figure, as in angels and souls, which should be conceived not as points but with a spiritual magnitude.
claims: (Reported) Angels and souls have positive spiritual magnitude.

ol96b1-277864-d1e879.summary: Fourth simplicity: positive spiritual magnitude that is infinite, the divine simplicity, which implies immensity. By this infinite spiritual magnitude God reaches every creature and is everywhere.
claims: (Reported) God's simplicity includes infinite spiritual magnitude, by which he reaches all creatures.

ol96b1-277864-d1e900.summary: Rubric naming Durand's opinion (Sentences I d. 37 q. 2).

ol96b1-277864-d1e905.summary: States Durand's view: beyond being in things by operation, God is said to be there by essence and presence, because operation requires his real coexistence with the creature, as a seal's figure is not made or kept in water without the seal's real coexistence. This coexistence is not position but order, since what is position in bodies is order in spirits (Augustine). This order of God to creatures is the presence by which God is present to every creature.
claims: (Reported) Divine operation presupposes God's real coexistence with creatures.
(Reported) This coexistence is an order, not a position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e936.summary: Rubric introducing the opinion of certain others.

ol96b1-277864-d1e941.summary: States the view that place properly has four functions (to circumscribe, conserve, define and hold present the located) and that four kinds of things are in place accordingly.
claims: (Reported) Place circumscribes, conserves, defines and holds present.

ol96b1-277864-d1e954.summary: First: natural bodies are in place under all four conditions.

ol96b1-277864-d1e965.summary: Second: mathematical bodies are imagined in place under three conditions, without conservation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e975.summary: Third: created spirits are in place under two conditions only, being present to it and defined there.

ol96b1-277864-d1e984.summary: Fourth: God is in place only under the last condition, presence. This presence is not position but a simultaneity, a real relation on the creature's side terminating at the divine essence under its absolute character; in spirits presence to place is a real relation in both extremes.
claims: (Reported) God's presence in place is a simultaneity, a real relation in the creature only.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1004.summary: Rubric introducing Auriol's view, beginning with the thesis, against the second and last opinions, that God's presence to things cannot be a simultaneity or relation of simultaneity.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1017.summary: Announces that Auriol's view will be given in five propositions.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1024.summary: First proposition: the presence by which God is in things by essence cannot be a relation of simultaneity between divine and created entity. Simultaneity requires a foundation in which the things are together (time, position, space, or something else). Deity and creature are together in nothing: not in time (shown earlier), not in position or place (God abstracts from both), and 'together in the simultaneity itself' is empty, since what things are together in founds the simultaneity and cannot be the simultaneity.
claims: Simultaneity requires a common foundation in which things are together.
God and creatures share no such foundation of time, position or place.
God's presence by essence cannot be a relation of simultaneity.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1076.summary: Confirms: if a body were not in place, like the outermost sphere, God could not be together with it in place, since it is not in place, nor in anything else except perhaps in being, since both are beings, which does not suffice for presence. So 'real simultaneity' or 'real presence' in this sense means nothing.
claims: Being together in being does not amount to presence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1099.summary: Further argument: nothing can be conceived as together with another unless it is understood to be where the other is. Simultaneity presupposes that both are 'here' and are subjects of position, so it holds only between positioned things in the same 'here'. Simultaneity does not make something be in place but presupposes it, and God is not a subject of position (or he would locate himself), so his being in creatures is not simultaneity.
claims: Simultaneity presupposes that both relata are in place.
God is not a subject of position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1136.summary: Further argument by dilemma: a relation of coexistence in creatures would be founded on them as things or as positioned. As things, it makes them together only in being things, which holds between east and west and the most distant things and does not suffice for presence.
claims: Coexistence founded on mere being does not amount to presence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1169.summary: Continues: nor can it be founded on creatures as positioned, since a relation founded on something as positioned terminates at another positioned thing, as likeness in whiteness terminates at another white thing. God is not positioned, so no such presence holds between God and creatures.
claims: A relation founded on position terminates only at a positioned thing.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1193.summary: Further argument: whatever is conceived as abstracted from every boundary, having no inside or outside in its reality and conceived only quidditatively, necessarily abstracts from simultaneity with anything positioned, since such simultaneity would give it an inside and outside. God abstracts thus, like the rose's character taken simply, so he cannot be conceived as coexisting with positioned things.
claims: What has no inside or outside cannot be simultaneous with positioned things.
God, like a quiddity taken simply, abstracts from all position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1232.summary: Rubric announcing the second proposition: this presence cannot be a relation of order, as the fourth opinion (Durand) holds.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1239.summary: Second proposition: God's presence cannot be a relation of order. Such an order would be causal (efficient, final or formal dependence) or positional (in, beside, below, before or behind), and neither applies.
claims: God's presence is neither a causal nor a positional order.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1260.summary: Not causal order: even if God were not in things, causal order would remain, so God's being in things is not formally things being from him, toward him, or below him in nobility.
claims: Causal order does not constitute God's being in things.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1273.summary: Not positional order: God's presence to a stone would then place him beside or below it, and 'beside' and 'below' are differences of position (Physics III; Averroes), so God would be positioned.
claims: Positional relations imply that God is positioned.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1295.summary: Further: order in general seems to be just a relation (habitudo). The view means either that presence is some relation in general or some special relation called order; either way it is insufficiently stated.
claims: 'Order' is either too general or left unspecified.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1313.summary: First horn: 'relation in general' is too general and confused.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1320.summary: Second horn: they do not say what kind of relation the order is, especially since God's being in a creature is not formally God being ordered to the creature or vice versa; being is not formally being-ordered, as the terms show.
claims: Being in something is not formally being ordered to it.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1338.summary: Rubric announcing the third proposition: presence cannot formally be God's operation terminating at the creature, as the first opinion (Thomas) says.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1350.summary: Third proposition: God's presence in creatures cannot formally be his operation in them (containing, conserving, giving being). Then his being in them by essence would be the same as by power, and a thing is said metaphorically to be where its power shines through its action, as a king is said to be in every part of his realm. But being everywhere by essence means more than this metaphorical shining of power.
claims: Presence by essence is not formally presence by operation.
Presence by operation alone is metaphorical, like a king's presence in his realm.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1396.summary: Confirmed by Lombard, who rebukes those who said God is in things by substance because by his substance's power he makes places and their contents exist and keeps working in them; Lombard says more must be understood in 'everywhere by essence' than a living person can grasp.
claims: Lombard rejects reducing presence by essence to causal power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1420.summary: Further argument: if operating on creatures and being in them were the same, either could answer the same question; formal identity is judged by questions (quantity answers 'how much', quality 'of what kind'). To 'where is God?' one does not properly answer 'he creates or conserves', nor to 'what does he do?' 'he is everywhere'.
claims: Formal identity can be tested by what question a predicate answers.
'Where' and 'what does he do' are different questions, so presence and operation differ.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1453.summary: Further argument: Augustine (De Trinitate VIII) distinguishes 'creator without place' from 'wholly everywhere', which he would not if they were formally the same.
claims: Augustine distinguishes being creator from being everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1469.summary: Rubric announcing the fourth proposition: positive spiritual magnitude does not explain God's being in place, as the third opinion (Richard) imagines.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1478.summary: Fourth proposition: positive magnitude does not explain how God is everywhere. It is either extensive magnitude, which is formally quantity and dimension and wholly repugnant to God, or intensive magnitude of nobility, as wisdom is called great (Augustine: in things not great in bulk, greater means better). Intensive magnitude has nothing to do with being in many places: more intense whiteness does not need more place (Liber sex principiorum: whiteness is not purer in a horse's hoof than in a pearl).
claims: Extensive magnitude is quantity and repugnant to God.
Intensive magnitude does not entail occupying more places.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1531.summary: Confirmed by Augustine (to Dardanus, De praesentia Dei): we should not think of God as spread through all things by a kind of bulk, as light is diffused, but as greatness is in two wise men, one greater than the other.
claims: God's greatness is not spatial diffusion (Augustine).

ol96b1-277864-d1e1547.summary: Further: even granting God spiritual magnitude, one must still say what it is for it to be everywhere, by contact, presence, simultaneity, coexistence or the like, and all of these have been shown impossible.
claims: Spiritual magnitude still needs an account of presence, and the candidate accounts fail.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1569.summary: Rubric announcing the fifth proposition: God is in things not by any positive condition of the located toward place, but by retaining one negative condition, complete non-distance from place.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1585.summary: Fifth proposition: the located thing has many positive conditions toward its place, but God is said to be in place by none of them, only because he retains one negative condition the located has toward place: non-distance (indistantia).
claims: God is in place by non-distance, a negative condition, not by any positive relation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1603.summary: Begins the explanation: the located has many conditions toward place, the first being that it touches it.
claims: Contact is the first condition of the located toward place.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1612.summary: Lists further conditions. Simultaneity with place is unity in position (extremes one by contact), from which come presence or coexistence; then being circumscribed by place, shaped by it, conserved in it, and not distant from it. Non-distance can occur by positing the opposite relation, nearness, as with a located body that touches its place, or without positing any opposite relation, so that the non-distant thing is neither near nor touching nor remote, abstracting from all position and incapable of nearness, distance, simultaneity or remoteness, all relations founded on position.
claims: Simultaneity is unity in position.
Non-distance can occur either with nearness or without any positional relation.
Nearness, distance and simultaneity are founded on position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1663.summary: Applies this: God cannot relate to the world-machine by any positive relation of the located to place (contact, simultaneity, presence, nearness, coexistence, being within or intimate), since all are founded on position and require both relata to be positioned.
claims: God has no positive locational relation to the world.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1683.summary: God therefore keeps the privation of the opposite of all these: he is not distant from the whole world or any part, not removed or outside, but wholly non-distant. He is not thereby near, within or together, since he abstracts from positive relations, leaving only the negation of distance and remoteness that the located also has, together with its opposite positive relation.
claims: God is wholly non-distant from the world without being near, within or together with it.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1707.summary: So being everywhere posits no positive relation in God, only the negation of one: complete non-distance from all things. It does not formally say God is not within things, not coexistent or not near (that would remove every condition of the located), but retains the one condition the located has, complete non-remoteness. This non-distance is a kind of presence, intimacy or simultaneity, though not positive, which is why Scripture's statements that God is intimate to, coexistent with and present to all things are granted.
claims: Being everywhere is complete non-distance, not a positive relation.
Non-distance does not deny God's being within things; it abstracts from it.
Scripture's language of intimacy and presence is true in the sense of non-distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1757.summary: First objection: what is not numerically distinct cannot be kept one without the other, and in the located, non-distance from place is just nearness, the negation of distance being founded on nearness. So God cannot keep non-distance without nearness and simultaneity.
claims: (Objection) Non-distance is identical with nearness.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1783.summary: Further objections. On this view being everywhere is not being distant from anything, but an angel, every spiritual creature, and every abstract objective concept (unity, rose taken simply, virtue, justice) is neither near nor distant, so all would be everywhere, which is erroneous since being everywhere is proper to God. And if being everywhere means God is not distant, it should equally mean he is not near, since he is neither; but being everywhere does not mean not being near all things, against the saints.
claims: (Objection) Angels and abstract concepts would be everywhere.
(Objection) By parity, being everywhere would mean not being near.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1827.summary: Further objection: no positive formal character consists in a negation, and 'being in' is positive, so the view contradicts itself by making being-in consist in not-being-in.
claims: (Objection) A positive formality cannot consist in a negation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1844.summary: Further objection: Augustine says God not only is not absent to things but is present to them (adest), so being everywhere means more than non-distance or non-absence.
claims: (Objection) Augustine affirms positive presence, not mere non-absence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1860.summary: Auriol maintains his view and cites the saints for it. Augustine (83 Questions): God is not somewhere; rather all things are in him. Hilary: God is a living power nowhere not present and nowhere lacking, so believed everywhere since he is lacking to none. Augustine on John: God is he who is nowhere lacking. These ways of speaking show the saints mean that being everywhere is not a positive relation but only not being distant from or absent to anything, since they sometimes say God is nowhere and sometimes in all things. (The text is partly corrupt and displaced.)
claims: The saints' language implies that omnipresence is non-absence, not a positive relation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1902.summary: Clarifies (in a badly corrupted text): abstracting from both distance and nearness differs from being determined to the negation of distance. 'Being in' is determined to non-distance, and something must determine God to it, namely operation reaching creatures' innermost being. A thing sustained by a power must be conceived as with that power either distant, near, or at least non-distant, since operation is not distant from the power from which it flows. A positively near power would be positioned, so the divine power is determined by operation as non-distant without contact, nearness, coexistence or simultaneity.
claims: Being-in is determinate non-distance, not mere abstraction from distance.
Operation requires that its power be non-distant from it.
Divine operation determines God to non-distance from all he conserves.

ol96b1-277864-d1e1993.summary: Finds this view in John Damascene, who says God is said to be in place where his operation is manifest, passes unmixed through all and gives all his operation, the place of an incorporeal nature being where it operates; so being everywhere and operating everywhere belong to God alone. Also in Aristotle (Physics VIII): the mover is in the part of the mobile that moves fastest, which Averroes explains as being where its effect appears, nearness to the mover being understood in being, not in place, since what is not in a body is not in place.
claims: Damascene places God where his operation is manifest.
Aristotle and Averroes locate the separate mover where its effect appears, by being, not place.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2054.summary: So according to these authorities, the formal character of the location of separate substances is a special non-distance that operation requires in the power from which it flows. They are located by operation not formally but as co-requiring, manifesting, or rather determining it. Only God can be everywhere and non-distant from all things, since he can act everywhere and reaches every effect by omnipotence, while an angel acts only on certain effects and so is not non-distant from all.
claims: Separate substances are located by a non-distance that their operation requires.
Only God is non-distant from all things, because only he can operate everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2091.summary: Replies to the first objection: it shows that the numerical non-distance founded on two bodies' nearness cannot be separated from that nearness, not that there cannot be another negation of distance without nearness.
claims: Non-distance without nearness is possible.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2108.summary: Replies to the second objection: not any non-distance from all things makes God everywhere, but the non-distance that operation determines and requires in its power. An angel does not have that toward all things, since it does not act on all.
claims: Only operational non-distance from all things constitutes being everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2128.summary: Replies to the third objection: operation does not require in its power the negation of nearness; it requires nearness in bodies, or at least non-absence and non-distance in abstract things.
claims: Operation requires nearness in bodies and non-distance in separate substances.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2141.summary: Replies to the fourth objection (from Augustine's 'adest'): what is hard to understand is hard to express and needs many circumlocutions, and separating non-distance from nearness is very hard because imagination usually dominates the abstractive power. Hence Lombard says divine location exceeds human ingenuity, and Augustine sometimes says God is everywhere because not lacking to anything (negatively) and sometimes that he is present (positively), though there is truly no positive relation but only non-distance. Since only the non-distance operation requires makes God everywhere, and in bodies operation requires its power to be near and assisting, God is said to be present to all. End of the first article.
claims: The difficulty of conceiving non-distance without nearness explains the saints' varied language.
Imagination usually dominates abstract thought.
God is said to be 'present' by analogy with bodily operation.

ol96b1-277864-Dd1e2201.summary: Asks whether God's omnipresence can be demonstrated from his operation or omnipotence. Opinions: Thomas and Durand (operation shows the power present, and God's power is his essence); Scotus (operation does not show presence, so omnipresence is only believed, with Lombard's disjunctive argument); and others who argue from omnipotence and immutability, which Auriol faults for omitting that God could be wholly abstract and for ignoring that a real relation of presence could be added or removed without change in God. Auriol's four propositions. (1) Operation does not demonstrate positive presence, simultaneity or intimacy, since the heavens are moved by a wholly abstract power, and presence is positional (Averroes' 'nearness in being' means non-distance). (2) Against Scotus, operation does demonstrate that the power is not distant: distance prevents action, every distant power is positioned and acts by contact or diffusion through the medium, acting follows being, and a power limited by finite distance must act through each part. (3) Scotus's arguments for action at a distance fail: the sun induces substantial forms through alteration by its ray, the form following as the terminus of alteration, educed from matter as its completion (with the principle of equivocal causality limited to creation); the sun's power penetrates the earth; the will causes while non-distant; and the philosophers' movers are non-distant from what they move. (4) Given the faith-held premise of universal conservation, it follows demonstratively, on supposition, that God is everywhere by complete non-distance, on the model of Aristotle's locating the first mover in Physics VIII.
claims: Operation does not demonstrate positive presence.
Operation does demonstrate that its power is not distant.
No created power acts immediately at a distance; action diffuses through the medium.
Substantial forms are educed through alteration as its terminus.
Given universal conservation (held by faith), God's omnipresence by non-distance is demonstrable on supposition.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2214.summary: Heading of the second article: whether it can be demonstrated from omnipotence that God is in all things, beginning with the opinion of Thomas (ST I q. 8 a. 3) and Durand.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2225.summary: States the view that God's being everywhere can be concluded because he operates everywhere by omnipotence, giving and conserving being. Operation necessarily shows its power present and intimate to its effect, and God's power and essence are the same, so his essence is present everywhere.
claims: (Reported) Operation demonstrates the presence of the operating power, and in God power is essence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2251.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio I d. 37 q. 1).

ol96b1-277864-d1e2257.summary: States Scotus's view: operation does not prove God present to things, since a power can reach by operation where it is not (as argued in the first article). God's being everywhere is not demonstrable but only believed, attested by Scripture, the saints and Lombard's argument: God cannot be nowhere (what is nowhere is nothing), nor somewhere and not elsewhere (he could then move, against his perfection), so he is everywhere.
claims: (Reported) Omnipresence cannot be demonstrated from operation and is held by faith.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2292.summary: Rubric introducing the opinion of certain others.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2297.summary: States the view that omnipresence can be demonstrated from omnipotence differently: omnipotence can do whatever implies no contradiction. Once a thing exists, God is either necessarily present to it essentially or can be not present.
claims: (Reported) Omnipotence can ground a proof of omnipresence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2319.summary: Continues: the second option fails, since if God could be not present and later present, this would occur by change in the creature or in God.
claims: (Reported) Becoming present requires a change in God or creature.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2330.summary: Continues: not by change in God, who is necessarily immutable, and not in the creature, which already existed, so God was necessarily in it. Otherwise God could change, or would not be omnipotent (unable to make himself present), or is always necessarily and immutably in the thing; the first two are impossible, so the third follows.
claims: (Reported) God is necessarily and immutably present to every existing thing.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2361.summary: Auriol says this procedure fails in two ways.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2369.summary: First flaw: it omits a fourth option, that God is so abstract as to be in no way present to things. That would not compromise omnipotence, any more than being unable to make himself a stone does. Philosophers would say an abstract thing is nowhere, and truly an abstract thing has no positive presence, only negative non-distance; positing it present would position it and make it a body, and God's inability to make himself a body does not limit his omnipotence.
claims: The argument omits that God could be wholly abstract and not positively present.
Positive presence would make God positioned and bodily.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2408.summary: Second flaw: those who posit real presence would say it is a real relation in the creature terminating at God, coming from outside and immediately acquirable, as the relation of 'where' is gained and lost with no absolute change. So God could by omnipotence newly impress or remove it, becoming present or not without change in himself, just as on their view an angel makes itself present to this or that body because that relation falls under its will.
claims: On the real-relation view, God could make himself present or absent without changing.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2450.summary: Rubric for Auriol's view: first, against the first opinion, God's general conserving operation does not demonstrate positive presence, coexistence or simultaneity with things. Then announces four propositions.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2468.summary: First proposition: operation does not demonstrate that the operating power is present, simultaneous, coexistent or positively present to the operation or its effect. However positioned the operation, it does not show its power to be bodily or positioned; otherwise the heavens could not be moved by an immaterial power, against Physics VIII, which shows the heaven's infinite motion requires a wholly incorporeal power abstracted from here and there. If bodily operation showed its power coexistent with or intimately within the body, the power would be positioned, since being within or simultaneously present is formally being in the same position. So a power can be wholly abstract, neither within nor outside the body, and still move it immediately.
claims: Operation does not prove positive presence of the operating power.
An immaterial power can move a body without being within or outside it.
Being within or simultaneously present is formally being in the same position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2536.summary: Possible reply: presence is not positional, though intimacy is, so presence of an abstract power to part of a body can be proved from operation; it is founded on being, not position, as abstract things can be present to abstract things (Averroes, Physics VIII: nearness to the mover in being, not place). (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: (Objection) Presence is founded on being, not position.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2571.summary: Replies: presence is a positional relation, so two abstract things cannot be grasped as mutually present. Presence is nearness without a medium, as absence is remoteness with intervening distance; if the bodily world were destroyed, only by phantasm could one think angels distant or near. Averroes uses 'approaching', which expresses a positional relation, but takes nearness privatively, as non-distance.
claims: Presence is nearness without medium, a positional relation.
Without bodies, angels are neither near nor distant except in imagination.
Averroes' 'nearness in being' means non-distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2609.summary: Rubric announcing the second proposition, against the second opinion (Scotus): operation necessarily shows that the power it flows from lacks the relation of distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2618.summary: Second proposition: operation necessarily proves the operating power not remote or distant; the relation of distance prevents operation. Every power subject to distance is positioned, every positioned thing acts by contact (being bodily and quantified), and an agent acting by contact lacks distance while acting, contact being simultaneity opposed to distance. So every operation is from a non-distant power.
claims: Distance prevents operation.
Every power subject to distance is positioned and acts by contact.
Every operation is from a non-distant power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2653.summary: Further proof: if an operation came from a distant power, the operation would be more abstract than the power. If it proceeded positionally and linearly, it would extend across the whole intervening space, so the power would not be distant from the operation (which is why distant action is seen to alter the medium). If not, the mode of acting would abstract from space while the power is positioned, making the mode of acting nobler than the power, which is impossible, since acting follows being.
claims: Acting follows being, so a positioned power cannot act non-positionally.
Distant action requires diffusion through the medium.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2721.summary: Further proof: if a power could act immediately on something at some distance, it could at infinite distance. If distance does not impede and simultaneity is not required, intervening space is accidental to the operation, and varying an accident does not change what is per se (a musician who builds remains a builder). But neither the sun nor any created power could act at an infinite distance, so none acts immediately at a distance.
claims: If distance were accidental to action, a power could act at any distance.
No created power can act at infinite distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2763.summary: Further proof: if a power is limited by a finite distance beyond which it cannot act, it regards every part of that distance, since a whole consists of parts, and regarding each part is reaching it by operation, so it alters the whole space, acting first on the contiguous part and then on the rest. So a power limited by finite distance is limited by any distance unless it first reaches the contiguous part; if its operation did not diffuse, no finite distance would limit it, and the sun could induce a substantial form in disposed matter at infinite distance.
claims: A power limited by distance acts through each part of the medium.
Only diffusion through the medium explains distance-limited action.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2848.summary: Explains: every bodily power reaches only to a certain distance because it diffuses its action through the medium, reaching the near part first and the remote part through it, and action weakens with distance until it fails. If a power acted immediately at a distance, its action would be no weaker far away than near, and no distance would limit it. Since no positioned, bodily power acts at every distance, none acts immediately at a distance; a bodily agent acts by touching the patient's surface, and there is no first part immediately reached, since any part is divisible, so there is no first instant of being changed.
claims: Bodily action weakens with distance because it diffuses through the medium.
No bodily power acts immediately at a distance.
There is no first part reached or first instant of change.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2914.summary: Answers the reply that this holds for bodily powers but not divine or spiritual ones: every distant power is necessarily bodily and positioned, since distance is a relation founded on positioned, quantified things.
claims: Only bodily, positioned things can be distant.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2934.summary: Rubric announcing the third proposition: the arguments of the first article's second opinion (Scotus) for immediate action at a distance are not effective.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2947.summary: Third proposition: the arguments that something can act immediately on what is distant from the form by which it acts do not hold.
claims: The arguments for immediate action at a distance fail.

ol96b1-277864-d1e2960.summary: Answers Scotus's first argument (the sun induces substantial forms immediately by its form). It falsely assumes that substantial forms are introduced directly by the sun's form rather than through heat generated by the ray. Then generation of the substantial form would not be the end of alteration but two separate actions, and generation would be per se, against Averroes (Physics VI): indivisible changes are not per se but are ends of divisible changes, as a column becomes right by local motion. No agent reaches an indivisible change immediately; it reaches it through the divisible change whose term it is. The mover makes the column right only by moving it, the builder induces the house's form by moving stones, and the seal shapes wax by moving its parts. So the agent inducing a substantial form does so by altering, the form following as figure follows the arrangement of parts. Averroes: since substantial form admits no more and less, change continues in proper accidents until the form is induced (blood to flesh in no time); motion generates heat and fire (De caelo II). So the sun's ray induces light, then proportional heat and all proper accidents, and with them the form, by one action, as Aristotle compares the generation of substances and figures (Physics VII). What is first in the agent's intention is last in execution. Position is a proper attribute of quantity answering 'where', and figure, a term of quantity, answers 'of what kind', so they are formally distinct. (Parts are corrupt.)
claims: Substantial forms are induced through alteration, as its terminus.
Indivisible changes are not per se but ends of divisible changes (Averroes).
No agent immediately reaches an indivisible change.
The substantial form follows the induction of its proper accidents, as figure follows the arrangement of parts.
Position and figure are formally distinct.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3205.summary: Concludes the reply: the sun does not induce forms by its substantial form without the ray. By altering through the ray it induces all the proper accidents of the form to be generated and the form as a consequence, as the builder induces the house's form by local motion, not by a further action after disposing. The end, as an indivisible term like the point of a line, is reached immediately by that of which it is the end, so alteration reaches the generation of the form. What is acquired by consequence can exceed its means, or motion could not generate fire. 'An equivocal effect does not exceed its cause' holds only of effects wholly produced, as in creation, where the effect is virtually contained in the agent; in natural change, which only draws matter from potency to act, the form is not virtually contained in the active qualities but is a completion. Hence Averroes (Metaphysics XI): like produces like not by its form directly but by drawing potency into act, so fire is generated by motion as by fire. Natural agents only perfect and complete. This is the 'latency' or 'inchoation' of forms, which is nothing but matter itself: fire is inchoate in air through something of itself (matter), and motion completes it. (More in the treatise on physical principles and in book 2.)
claims: The sun induces forms by altering through its ray.
An effect acquired by consequence can exceed its proximate means.
The principle that an equivocal effect does not exceed its cause holds only for total production (creation).
Natural agents do not make forms as wholes but complete what is inchoate in matter.
The 'inchoation' of forms is matter itself.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3372.summary: Answers Scotus's second argument (the sun acts in the earth's depths and from the other hemisphere). The sun's power does reach the earth's interior: either the ray itself, which can penetrate even to the center since every element, earth included, has some transparency (or it would lack its own light and visible quality); or an insensible quality carried with light, as Averroes suggests (De caelo II); or heat from rays reflected at the surface, altering further down to where minerals form. The sun in the other hemisphere generates and conserves plants and humans here through qualities left by its daily course or rays reflected from the moon and stars, which all receive some light from the sun.
claims: The sun's power penetrates to where minerals form, by ray, carried quality, or propagated heat.
The sun affects the other hemisphere through residual qualities or reflected light.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3438.summary: Answers Scotus's third argument (the omnipotent causes by will): the omnipotent so causes that it is neither near nor distant from what it causes, being wholly abstract but entirely non-distant. So no power acts on what is distant from it.
claims: God causes by will while non-distant from his effects.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3460.summary: Answers Scotus's fourth argument (operation is prior to presence): it assumes God is present by positive intimacy, which would be separable from operation as something prior. But since presence is only non-distance, which operation determines regarding its power, God cannot be grasped as operating without at once being grasped as non-distant.
claims: God cannot be conceived as operating without being conceived as non-distant.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3482.summary: Answers Scotus's fifth argument (the philosophers' placeless supreme mover). Aristotle and Averroes never said an intelligence moves an orb without being in it in the sense of negative non-distance. Aristotle says God is in heaven (De caelo I), and Averroes explains this differs from a body in place, as Physics VIII shows. Also, for the philosophers the first principle does not move as efficient executor, only the conjoined intelligence, the orb's mover, does; so the argument does not show that an efficient mover is not always non-distant.
claims: Aristotle places God in heaven, but not as a body in place.
For the philosophers the first principle moves not as executor but via conjoined intelligences.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3526.summary: Adds that since for the philosophers the first principle moves by causing desire in the conjoined mover, it is understood as non-distant from that mover, so they placed it in the same part of the orb by non-distance.
claims: The first principle is non-distant from the conjoined mover it moves by desire.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3544.summary: Answers Scotus's sixth argument (transition between contradictories): presence is not positive but only negation, so it is understood together with the flowing of operation from the power.
claims: Non-distance is co-understood with the flow of operation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3555.summary: Answers Scotus's seventh argument (Physics VII concerns bodies): granted 'agent and patient are together' holds only for bodies acting by contact, it is generally true that operation is non-distant from its power, bodily or abstract; in bodily powers simultaneity and contact are also required, not mere negative non-distance.
claims: Operation is always non-distant from its power, bodily or not.
Bodily powers additionally require contact.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3578.summary: Answers Scotus's last argument (order of powers or imperfection explains action through a medium): the sun does not induce forms after diffusing its ray because of an order of active powers or progression from imperfect to perfect; operation is more perfect nearer, given a recipient. The reason is that alteration leads to the substantial form as moving wax leads to the seal's figure. So every agent is non-distant from its operation, contiguous in bodies and non-distant in abstract forms.
claims: Action through a medium is explained by alteration leading to form, not by order or imperfection of powers.
Every agent is non-distant from its operation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3617.summary: Rubric announcing the fourth proposition: God's universal conservation of all things proves demonstratively that he is non-distant from all by essence, and so everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3633.summary: Fourth proposition: God's universal sustaining operation in all things demonstratively concludes that he is everywhere by non-distance, not because this sustaining is known by natural light, but, once held by faith and supposed true, a demonstrative argument follows. No operation can flow from a power conceived as distant (proved), and need not flow from one necessarily near (also proved), so operation forces the intellect to grasp its power as non-distant. The operation conserving things is intimate to each, so the divine power must be conceived as non-distant from each thing's innermost being; and God's power is his real essence, so God is necessarily grasped as really and essentially non-distant from every creature.
claims: Given universal conservation (held by faith), God's omnipresence follows demonstratively.
Operation forces the intellect to conceive its power as non-distant.
God's power is his essence, so he is essentially non-distant from all creatures.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3688.summary: Shows the argument is demonstrative: a proposition that, with another known by natural light, demonstrates simply, demonstrates on supposition when joined to a premise supposed true. Aristotle and Averroes (Physics VIII) demonstrate the first mover's location from 'a power cannot be distant from its operation' plus 'the mover's operation is greatest in the great circle dividing the sphere': the mover is there by complete non-distance, where its operation shines most (fastest motion), not positionally. Likewise, with the premise from faith that God's operation shines in all things, conserving them intimately, it follows demonstratively, on supposition, that God is everywhere by complete non-distance, not positionally. End of the second article.
claims: A demonstration can be valid on supposition of a premise held by faith.
Aristotle's location of the first mover is a model for the proof.
Given faith in universal conservation, God is demonstrably everywhere by non-distance.

ol96b1-277864-Dd1e3759.summary: Examines the traditional modes by which God is in things (essence, presence, power, and in some by grace). Thomas's account (grace as object known and loved; power, presence and essence answering Manichees, deniers of providence and those who limited creation, illustrated by a king) is criticized: God dwells actually in infants who do not know him and only in the holy; presence by knowledge would put things in God rather than God in things; a king's presence by power is metaphorical; and presence as cause of being collapses into power. Scotus's (power as conserving, presence as knowing, essence as infinite entering) fails because entering reduces to conserving or is positional, God's knowledge does not change with creation, and infinity is a cause of omnipresence, not omnipresence. Durand's (substance, power, operation) yields four modes, and the coexistence-without-medium view is circular and positional. Auriol's four propositions: essence, presence and power are three aspects of one mode, essence the substrate, presence (negative non-distance) the formal character, and power (actual or possible operation) the determinant. Asking which is prior is superfluous, since non-distance is a relative negation whose prerequisites are essence, operation and creature. Immensity is deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place, distinct from infinity; illapsus is non-absence from creatures' innermost being; God contains all because creatures' non-distance stems from their dependence. Presence by grace is the same mode intensified by God's singular operation of infusing and conserving grace, as the celestial mover is singularly in the fastest circle, while God's presence in Christ is non-distance required by the hypostatic union.
claims: Essence, presence and power are substrate, formal character and determinant of one mode of omnipresence.
Omnipresence formally is negative non-distance.
Immensity is deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place.
All things are in God rather than he in them because of their dependence.
Presence by grace is the same mode, singularized by the intense operation of grace.
God's presence in Christ is non-distance required by the hypostatic union.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3772.summary: Heading of the third article: whether the four modes (God in things by essence, presence and power, and in some by grace) are well assigned, beginning with Thomas's opinion (ST I q. 8 a. 3).

ol96b1-277864-d1e3781.summary: States Thomas's account. God is in things in two ways: as object in the operator (the known in the knower, the desired in the desirer), and so specially in rational creatures by grace, by which they know and love him actually or habitually; and as agent cause in effects, in all things. A king is in his whole realm by power, though not present everywhere, and present to all he sees, though not by substance in every part of the house; so power, presence and essence differ. Against the Manichees (not all is under God's power), God is everywhere by power; against deniers of providence, by presence (all is naked to his eyes); against those who held God created only the first creatures, by essence (present to all as cause of being).
claims: (Reported) God is in the rational creature by grace as object known and loved.
(Reported) God is in all things by power (subject to it), presence (seen by him) and essence (as cause of being).
(Reported) Each mode answers a specific error.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3862.summary: First criticism of Thomas: if God were in the saints by grace as object in the knower or lover, he would not actually be in those who do not actually know or love him, only habitually. But Augustine (to Dardanus) says God indwells some who do not know him, such as infants, and actually, since they are actually his temple. So presence by grace is not as object known or loved.
claims: God dwells actually in baptized infants who do not know him.
Presence by grace is not presence as object of knowledge or love.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3900.summary: Further: by grace God is only in the good and holy (Augustine), but as object known he is in many who are not holy.
claims: God is known by many unholy persons but dwells by grace only in the holy.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3911.summary: Further: Augustine says the soul, wholly present in each part of the body, acts more intensely in some parts than others, and Lombard (this distinction, ch. 2) says likewise that God, wholly in all things by essence, is said to be singularly in the saints because he acts more fully and intensely in them. So God is there by grace as spiritually operating, not as object known.
claims: God is in the saints by grace as more intensely operating.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3942.summary: Second criticism, on presence. Created things are not present to the divine gaze objectively and terminatively but denominatively, since only God's essence is present to him and in it every creature equivalently and eminently. If presence meant being known, God would be in his own essence by presence, which no one grants. And by cognized being the object is present in the knower, not the reverse, so things would be in God by presence rather than God in things. So presence cannot mean the presence of sight.
claims: Creatures are present to God's knowledge only denominatively, through his essence.
Presence by knowledge would make things present in God, not God in things.

ol96b1-277864-d1e3988.summary: Third criticism, on power: the king's presence by power is metaphorical and loose. The king is not properly in his realm by power, which acts through executors; his 'power' is there only as the subjects' grasp of his will and their obligation, a relation of reason. God cannot be said to be in things by power in this metaphorical way.
claims: A king's presence by power is metaphorical, a relation of reason.
God's presence by power is not metaphorical.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4021.summary: Fourth criticism, on essence: being present to all as cause of being is being present by power, which is supposed to be a distinct mode, so 'by essence' is badly assigned.
claims: 'Present as cause of being' collapses essence into power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4041.summary: Rubric naming Scotus's opinion (Ordinatio I d. 37 q. 1).

ol96b1-277864-d1e4047.summary: States Scotus's view: God can be considered in three ways.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4054.summary: First, as producing and conserving, so in things by power; second, as knowing, so by presence.
claims: (Reported) God is in things by power as conserving and by presence as knowing.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4065.summary: Third, by his infinity and unlimitedness, as he enters (illabitur) each thing intimately, so in things by essence. Auriol's first objection: the first mode collapses into the third, since God enters a creature only by producing and conserving its being, and any positive intimacy or entering would be a positional relation requiring God to be positioned and bodily.
claims: (Reported) God is in things by essence through his infinity and intimate entering.
Positive intimacy would make God positioned.
God enters creatures only by producing and conserving them.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4094.summary: Second objection to Scotus: God knows creatures no differently after they are made than before (Augustine, De Genesi V), yet he was not in them by presence before they were made, so presence is not by knowledge; besides, things would be present in God rather than the reverse. Third objection: infinity names a cause of God's being or being able to be everywhere, not his actually being in place; and 'entering' implies being intimately within, a positional relation, and intimate entering is just presence, so essence and presence are not well distinguished.
claims: God's knowledge of creatures does not change with their existence, so presence is not knowledge.
Infinity is the cause of omnipresence, not omnipresence itself.
Illapsus is positional or reduces to presence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4146.summary: Rubric naming Durand's opinion (Sentences I d. 37 q. 2).

ol96b1-277864-d1e4151.summary: States Durand's view: the modes are distinguished by three things on God's side as actually causing and conserving: substance, power and operation. Creation makes a thing exist and conservation continues it; existence presents the thing to God and so God to it, and since this presence is real exhibition, not just knowledge, God is in things by essence. Power does not differ from essence and operation flows from power, so he is in things by power.
claims: (Reported) The modes correspond to God's substance, power and operation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4191.summary: Objection to Durand: being by power and by operation would then count separately, giving four modes (operation, presence, real exhibition of essence, power), so the modes are not distinguished by these three.
claims: Durand's scheme yields four modes, not three.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4224.summary: Rubric introducing the opinion of certain others.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4229.summary: States the view that God is everywhere by power through causality (continuing and conserving all), and by presence through simultaneity, not of contact or duration but of presential coexistence of one essence with another. Such presence may concern extrinsic accidents (no medium between them) or innermost essences (no medium between them). Since God has no accidents, he coexists by essence, so the third mode, by essence, specifies the second.
claims: (Reported) Presence is coexistence without medium; essence specifies it as concerning innermost natures.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4286.summary: Objections: it assumes a positive coexistence or simultaneity between God and creatures, which are positional relations; it is circular, explaining presence by simultaneity and simultaneity by presence, though positive presence is intelligible only as simultaneity of duration or position; and it explains presence as lack of a medium, but a medium and its extremes are of one kind and exist only between positioned things.
claims: The view presupposes positional relations and is circular.
A medium exists only between positioned things.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4332.summary: Rubric for Auriol's view: first, power, presence and essence together express one single mode of God's being everywhere.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4351.summary: First proposition: the three do not express three modes but fully declare the one mode by which God is everywhere. The preposition 'per' expresses causality, and can signify the substrate said to be everywhere, the formal cause by which it is everywhere, or what determines that formality to the substrate.
claims: Essence, presence and power are three aspects of one mode, not three modes.
'Per' can express substrate, formal cause or determinant.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4371.summary: 'By essence' names the substrate in God of being everywhere, his essence. 'By presence' names what being everywhere formally is: a presence that is not positive but privative or negative, complete non-distance from all things.
claims: 'By essence' names the substrate of omnipresence.
'By presence' names its formal character, negative non-distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4397.summary: 'By power' does not mean God's power is everywhere as another mode (power and essence are the same in God, and power is everywhere only because essence is), nor the formality of being everywhere. It names what determines the formality to the substrate, non-distance to the essence: through power God's operation is grasped as necessarily reaching each thing's innermost being, and the essence from which it flows as non-distant from all. So God is everywhere by essence as substrate, by power as determinant and requirement, and by presence formally and quidditatively, presence always meaning negative non-distance. Where God is said to be in things in three ways, this refers to three factors in one mode, not three modes. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: 'By power' names what determines non-distance to God's essence.
God is everywhere by essence as substrate, by power as determinant, by presence formally.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4454.summary: Notes that not only power actualized in operation but operation understood as possible in some place shows that the substance of the operation is non-distant. Since God not only conserves creatures' innermost being but can act on them as he wills, his possible operation too determines his being everywhere. That is why one says 'by power' rather than 'by operation': operation possible or already actual, flowing or able to flow from power.
claims: Possible as well as actual operation determines God's non-distance.
'By power' covers both actual and possible operation.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4496.summary: Rubric announcing the second proposition: Scotus's inquiry into whether presence by essence and presence is posterior to and separable from presence by power is superfluous.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4512.summary: Second proposition: asking which mode precedes the other is superfluous. Some say being by power is prior to and of itself separable from being by essence and presence, inseparable in God only because of his infinity: a real relation presupposes its foundation, presence by essence is a real relation in the creature terminating at God, so it presupposes the creature, which presupposes God's operation (being by power). Auriol says this errs by treating presence as a real relation when it is only non-distance, and by treating being by power as a mode of being without presence, whereas without non-distance operation is in no way being in a place; it makes something be in place only by exhibiting the operator's power and essence as non-distant. The order is among requirements of one thing: the substrate and the determinant are understood first, then the term (essence, operation flowing from it, creature receiving it), and from these arises complete non-distance. Though not a positive relation, it is a relative negation, since negation reduces to the genus of the affirmation (Augustine, De Trinitate V: 'unbegotten' is said relatively like 'begotten'). So creature and operation precede non-distance not as one mode precedes another but as prerequisites of its formal element.
claims: Asking which mode of presence is prior is superfluous.
Operation without non-distance is not a mode of being in place.
Non-distance is a relative negation, not a positive relation.
Creature and operation precede non-distance as its prerequisites, not as a prior mode.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4639.summary: Rubric announcing what God's immensity, entering (illapsus) and containing mean, by which he fills, enters and contains all.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4650.summary: Third proposition: explains immensity, entering and containment from the foregoing. Immensity is not extensive magnitude filling length, breadth and depth (God abstracts from quantity), nor intensive magnitude like purer whiteness (that is infinity, which has no reference to places). So immensity differs from infinity and concerns place and creatures, but with no positive order: God is neither present by nearness, simultaneity or coexistence nor absent by distance, but wholly non-distant. Immensity is the force by which God necessarily cannot be absent from or distant to any place, actual or possible, even infinitely many. It is deity itself with a connotation, the impossibility of absence from any possible place, and belongs to God alone. Entering or intimacy is likewise non-absence, connoting the creature's innermost being: nothing intimate in a thing does not flow from deity, so God is as intimate to a creature as it is to itself. God contains all, and all are in him rather than he in them, because this non-distance arises from the creature's need: operation requires the power's non-absence, not the reverse, so God can exist without the creature but not the creature without God. As the located needs place and the contained the container, creatures' non-distance to God is like that of the located, and God's to creatures is like that of the container.
claims: Immensity is neither extensive nor intensive magnitude.
Immensity differs from infinity in referring to place.
Immensity is deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place.
God is as intimate to a creature as it is to itself, since all its innermost being flows from deity.
All things are in God rather than he in them, because their non-distance arises from their dependence.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4826.summary: Rubric announcing the fourth proposition: God's being in the rational creature by grace reduces to being by essence, presence and power, and his being in Christ by union reduces to being by essence and presence, but not by power.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4839.summary: Fourth proposition: God's being in rational creatures by grace reduces to the mode already described. Every operation requires non-distance of its power, but a more powerful and intense operation requires it more, so Aristotle places the mover in the heaven's greatest circle (Physics VIII): motion everywhere shows the mover non-distant from every part, but the fastest motion of the equinoctial circle shows it specially non-distant there. God is in all things by conserving operation, but acts more vehemently in rational creatures, not only for their natural being and well-being but for supernatural well-being through the gifts of grace he gives and conserves. So he is singularly non-distant from the saints, as the mover is singularly in the greatest circle though commonly in every part.
claims: More intense operation determines a more singular non-distance.
God acts more vehemently in rational creatures through grace.
God is singularly in the saints as the mover is singularly in the greatest celestial circle.

ol96b1-277864-d1e4911.summary: Further: God is singularly in things where his singular operation appears ('the finger of God is here', Exodus 8; Judith 13), and the infusion and conservation of grace is a singular operation beyond nature. So presence by grace is not specifically different from presence by essence, presence and power, though it differs numerically or by matter: what nature shows in all things, grace singularly does in the rational creature. God is in all things by the nature given them and in the saints by grace, as Lombard says (the soul acts more intensely in some parts). No need to say God is there by grace as object known or loved; this explains why he dwells by grace in infants and why he dwells only in those with grace. One may also say, as in the discussion of the Spirit's temporal procession, that God dwells objectively by grace as the lover in the beloved, but that mode is intentional and does not include non-distance. Moreover, God is singularly in the man Christ by essence and non-distance, required not by operation but by the hypostatic union, as the soul's formal effect of animating the body requires its non-distance without nearness or within-ness. Sustaining the humanity hypostatically requires the Word's, and so the whole deity's, singular non-distance (more in book 3). End of the third article.
claims: God is singularly present where his singular operation appears.
Presence by grace differs from general presence numerically, not specifically.
Presence by grace is not presence as object known or loved.
God is in Christ by non-distance required by the hypostatic union, not by operation.
The soul is in the body by non-distance required by its formal effect.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5050.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the objections.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5056.summary: Introduces the replies to the opening arguments.
