ol96b1-277864-d1e5063.summary: Replies to the non-reciprocity argument: place and located do not reciprocate in containment (a jar containing wine is not contained by it), but they do in presence and contact (place touches the located and vice versa), and likewise in non-distance or non-absence. So God can be in things and they in him. Paul's 'in him we live' and Bede's 'the angel is within God' hold because God's non-distance to things resembles that of a container, arising from the things' need, not God's.
claims: Containment is not reciprocal, but contact and non-distance are.
Things are in God as contained because their non-distance stems from their need.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5100.summary: Replies to the second argument: God is above all not positionally but in being, and is said to be nowhere because he lacks all position and simultaneity with things. This does not prevent his being everywhere by non-absence and complete non-distance.
claims: God is above all in being, not position.
God is nowhere by lack of position, yet everywhere by non-distance.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5116.summary: Replies to the time-and-place argument: God abstracts from both, but divine being necessarily connotes time, since no act, first or second, can be understood without duration as measure or as subject. Place is not so connoted: it is connoted as non-distant from divine being not because it is place but because it is produced and dependent. Eternity can also be said to connote time not as coexisting or simultaneous but negatively, as non-distant along the successive line of before and after.
claims: Divine being connotes duration, since every act implies duration.
Place is connoted only as produced and dependent.
Eternity relates to time by non-distance along succession.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5153.summary: Replies to the fourth through seventh arguments. Anselm means God is in no place positionally or by positive coexistence, only by non-absence and non-distance; likewise Augustine. The category 'where' covers position and relations founded on it (up, down, near, far, together), and also non-absence, the negation of the located's relation to place, so that sense of 'where' applies to God. God abstracts from every positive relation to place, as unity and the now do, but not from the relative negation of non-absence; no operation flows from unity or the now that would place them. Perhaps the now is everywhere, as Aristotle says time is in heaven and on earth (Physics IV), by non-distance to all it measures, but not as God is, since not all creatures are measured by time.
claims: Anselm and Augustine deny positional presence, not non-distance.
'Where' in the sense of non-absence applies to God.
God, unlike unity, operates and is therefore non-distant from things.
Time is everywhere by non-distance to what it measures, but not universally as God is.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5216.summary: Replies to the change argument: God does not change when he becomes non-absent through a new creation. He was not absent by anything positive but because the creature did not exist, so when it comes to be nothing is removed from God; a creature is posited to which he is not absent.
claims: God's becoming non-absent to new creatures involves no change in him.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5241.summary: Replies to the extrinsic-cause argument and the last one: God is not in things as cause in the sense that causing is formally existing in place. Causing requires non-distance of the causing essence, and so God's non-absence, in which being in place formally consists. This belongs to God though he is an efficient, extrinsic cause.
claims: Even an extrinsic efficient cause is non-distant from its effects.

ol96b1-277864-d1e5261.summary: Closing note: Lombard also mentions here the place and motion of created spirits and how the rational soul is wholly in each part of the body (perhaps not true of brute souls), but these are deferred to book 2, which treats creatures directly.
claims: Questions on angelic place and the soul's presence in the body are deferred to book 2.
